hook.en: We can price the timber in a forest. But what is the price of the oxygen it makes, the bees it shelters, or the joy of hearing a bird sing at dawn?
hook.kn: ಅರಣ್ಯದ ಮರಮುಟ್ಟಿಗೆ ಬೆಲೆ ಕಟ್ಟಬಹುದು. ಆದರೆ ಅದು ತಯಾರಿಸುವ ಆಮ್ಲಜನಕ, ಆಶ್ರಯ ನೀಡುವ ಜೇನುನೊಣಗಳು, ಮುಂಜಾನೆಯ ಹಕ್ಕಿಯ ಹಾಡಿನ ಆನಂದಕ್ಕೆ ಬೆಲೆ ಎಷ್ಟು?

objectives.en: Explain the narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian and ethical arguments for conservation

narration.en: We can price the timber in a forest. But what is the price of the oxygen it makes, the bees it shelters, or the joy of hearing a bird sing at dawn?
narration.kn: ಅರಣ್ಯದ ಮರಮುಟ್ಟಿಗೆ ಬೆಲೆ ಕಟ್ಟಬಹುದು. ಆದರೆ ಅದು ತಯಾರಿಸುವ ಆಮ್ಲಜನಕ, ಆಶ್ರಯ ನೀಡುವ ಜೇನುನೊಣಗಳು, ಮುಂಜಾನೆಯ ಹಕ್ಕಿಯ ಹಾಡಿನ ಆನಂದಕ್ಕೆ ಬೆಲೆ ಎಷ್ಟು?

body.en: The reasons for conserving biodiversity can be grouped into three categories: narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian and ethical. Narrowly utilitarian arguments are simple: humans derive countless direct economic benefits from nature, such as food (cereals, pulses, fruits), firewood, fibre, construction material, industrial products (tannins, lubricating oils, dyes, resins, perfumes) and products of medicinal importance. More than 25 per cent of the drugs currently sold in the market worldwide are derived from plants, and 25,000 species of plants contribute to the traditional medicines used by native peoples around the world. Nobody knows how many more medicinally useful plants exist in tropical rain forests waiting to be explored. With increasing resources put into "bioprospecting" (exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance), nations endowed with rich biodiversity can expect to reap enormous benefits.

points.en: Direct benefits: food, firewood, fibre, construction material, industrial products, medicines
>25% of drugs sold worldwide are derived from plants
25,000 plant species used in traditional medicines
Bioprospecting: exploring diversity for economically important products

narration.en: The narrowly utilitarian argument is about direct benefits: food, fibre, firewood, industrial products and medicines. More than a quarter of the drugs sold worldwide come from plants, and bioprospecting searches biodiversity for new valuable products.
narration.kn: ಸಂಕುಚಿತ ಉಪಯುಕ್ತತಾ ವಾದ ನೇರ ಲಾಭಗಳ ಬಗ್ಗೆ: ಆಹಾರ, ನಾರು, ಉರುವಲು, ಕೈಗಾರಿಕಾ ಉತ್ಪನ್ನಗಳು ಮತ್ತು ಔಷಧಗಳು. ವಿಶ್ವದಲ್ಲಿ ಮಾರಾಟವಾಗುವ ಔಷಧಗಳ ಕಾಲುಭಾಗಕ್ಕಿಂತ ಹೆಚ್ಚು ಸಸ್ಯಗಳಿಂದ ಬರುತ್ತವೆ; ಜೈವಿಕ ಶೋಧನೆ ಹೊಸ ಮೌಲ್ಯಯುತ ಉತ್ಪನ್ನಗಳನ್ನು ಹುಡುಕುತ್ತದೆ.

say.en: There are three kinds of reasons to conserve biodiversity: narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian and ethical.
Narrowly utilitarian: direct products such as food, fibre, wood and medicines. More than 25 per cent of drugs sold come from plants, and bioprospecting looks for more.
Broadly utilitarian: ecosystem services. The Amazon forest makes about 20 per cent of the oxygen in the air; bees, birds and bats pollinate our crops; nature gives us beauty.
Ethical: every species has an intrinsic value, whether or not it is useful to us, and we have a duty to pass it on to future generations.

text.en: More than 25 per cent of drugs sold worldwide come from plants
Bioprospecting: searching species for new products of economic value
Firewood, fibre, timber, resins and dyes from forests
The Amazon forest produces about 20 per cent of the oxygen in the atmosphere
Bees, birds and bats pollinate the crops that give us fruits and seeds
The pleasure of walking through a thick forest in bloom

explanation.en: Narrowly utilitarian: direct products we use (food, fibre, medicines, bioprospecting). Broadly utilitarian: services nature gives free (oxygen, pollination, aesthetic pleasure). Ethical: every species has an intrinsic value and we have a moral duty to pass it on.
explanation.kn: ಸಂಕುಚಿತ: ನೇರ ಉತ್ಪನ್ನಗಳು; ವಿಶಾಲ: ಪರಿಸರ ಸೇವೆಗಳು; ನೈತಿಕ: ಪ್ರತಿ ಪ್ರಭೇದಕ್ಕೂ ಸ್ವಂತ ಮೌಲ್ಯ.

body.en: The broadly utilitarian argument says that biodiversity plays a major role in many ecosystem services that nature provides. The fast-dwindling Amazon forest is estimated to produce, through photosynthesis, 20 per cent of the total oxygen in the Earth's atmosphere. Can we put an economic value on this service by nature? Pollination, without which plants cannot give us fruits or seeds, is another service, provided through pollinators: bees, bumblebees, birds and bats. There are other intangible benefits too: the aesthetic pleasures of walking through a thick woods, watching spring flowers in full bloom, or waking up to a bulbul's song in the morning. The ethical argument relates to what we owe to millions of plant, animal and microbe species with whom we share this planet. Philosophically or spiritually, we need to realise that every species has an intrinsic value, even if it may not be of any current or economic value to us. We have a moral duty to care for their well-being and pass on our biological legacy in good order to future generations.

points.en: Ecosystem services: Amazon forest makes ~20% of atmospheric oxygen
Pollination by bees, bumblebees, birds and bats
Ethical: every species has intrinsic value; duty to future generations

narration.en: Broadly, biodiversity provides ecosystem services: the Amazon forest makes about 20 per cent of the oxygen in our atmosphere, and bees, birds and bats pollinate our crops. Ethically, every species has intrinsic value and we owe it to future generations to protect it.
narration.kn: ವಿಶಾಲ ದೃಷ್ಟಿಯಲ್ಲಿ ಜೀವವೈವಿಧ್ಯ ಪರಿಸರ ಸೇವೆಗಳನ್ನು ನೀಡುತ್ತದೆ: ಅಮೆಜಾನ್ ಅರಣ್ಯ ವಾತಾವರಣದ ಸುಮಾರು 20% ಆಮ್ಲಜನಕ ತಯಾರಿಸುತ್ತದೆ, ಜೇನುನೊಣ, ಹಕ್ಕಿ, ಬಾವಲಿಗಳು ಪರಾಗಸ್ಪರ್ಶ ಮಾಡುತ್ತವೆ. ನೈತಿಕವಾಗಿ ಪ್ರತಿ ಪ್ರಭೇದಕ್ಕೂ ಅಂತರ್ಗತ ಮೌಲ್ಯವಿದೆ; ಮುಂದಿನ ಪೀಳಿಗೆಗೆ ಅದನ್ನು ಉಳಿಸುವುದು ನಮ್ಮ ಕರ್ತವ್ಯ.

problem.en: Classify each reason for saving the Western Ghats forests as narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian or ethical: (a) the forests give timber and medicinal plants; (b) forest insects pollinate the coffee and arecanut plantations nearby; (c) the lion-tailed macaque has a right to exist whether or not it is useful to us.

steps.en: (a) Direct products we harvest and sell: narrowly utilitarian.
(b) A service nature provides, pollination: broadly utilitarian.
(c) Intrinsic value of a species: ethical.
